rules: The lookup product combines HM Land Registry title numbers with Ordnance Survey AddressBase UPRNs.
It covers registered properties in England and Wales where an associated address contains a UPRN.
HM Land Registry records addresses during registration.
Registration addresses are linked to AddressBase data where a match can be made.
HM Land Registry creates an address where no suitable national address is found.
Created addresses and title numbers can be matched when corresponding AddressBase addresses later become available.
A title number and UPRN are linked only where a relationship between the AddressBase address and title can be established.
The lookup dataset is closely related to National Polygon and Title Descriptor products.
Those products are separated to make them smaller and easier to manage and maintain.
The title number is the identifier used to link the lookup data with other HM Land Registry products.
The documented lookup class contains Title Number and UPRN.
Title_No is documented as a character field.
UPRN is documented as an integer field.
UPRN is mandatory in a published lookup row.
Address searching, ingest and matching can create duplicate addresses when supplied information does not match LRPG.
A duplicate can leave one LRPG address with a title number but no UPRN and another with a UPRN but no title number.
An address can have a UPRN but no title association when it is absent from LRPG.
HM Land Registry created its first national address database in the 1990s.
That database was populated with Royal Mail residential Postcode Address File addresses.
Earlier addressing used street-card indexes and local gazetteers.
HM Land Registry moved to the Land Registry Property Gazetteer in 2002.
LRPG initially used Ordnance Survey AddressPoint as its national address base.
Where appropriate, customer addresses and title numbers were linked to AddressPoint addresses.
In 2011 HM Land Registry moved from AddressPoint to AddressLayer 2 after adopting Ordnance Survey MasterMap.
In 2014 AddressBase became the national address source.
LRPG ingests Post Office PAF data from AddressBase to maintain addressing consistency.
Post Office addresses excluded from AddressBase because they do not match local-authority addresses have no UPRN and are absent from this dataset.
Where a title affects many properties, all affecting UPRNs may be associated.
A title has no UPRN association when its AddressBase address has not been transferred into LRPG, even if a UPRN exists.
Planning authorities may start with incomplete or imperfect data and improve it over time.
The checking service accepts CSV data.
The checking service accepts GeoJSON data.
The checking service accepts GML data.
The checking service accepts GeoPackage data.
An endpoint URL can be submitted for checking.
Published planning data must be placed on the planning authority's official website.
Published data must be presented in a clear and understandable format.
The publication must include a statement that the data is provided under the Open Government Licence.
An endpoint URL is the location from which anyone can download the data.
An endpoint can be a file hosted on the authority's web server.
An endpoint can be a live API feed hosted by GIS or open-data software.
An ArcGIS layer endpoint contains the ArcGIS REST services path.
An ArcGIS layer endpoint identifies the service name.
An ArcGIS layer endpoint identifies a service type such as FeatureServer or MapServer.
An ArcGIS layer endpoint includes a number identifying the layer.
Data updates should be made at the existing endpoint URL.
The endpoint URL should not be changed merely because the data is updated.
Each dataset webpage must link to the endpoint URL.
Each dataset webpage must summarize what the data is about.
A unique documentation URL may be implemented with one webpage per record.
Multiple records may share a webpage when each record has its own anchor link.
The publishing system must support fragment identifiers when anchor links are used.
A legal-document record needs a document-url linking directly to the file.
Providing data to the platform requires the submitter's full name.
Providing data requires a work email address.
Providing data requires the public endpoint URL.
Providing data requires the official source webpage URL.
Creating a new endpoint URL requires the data to be provided again.
A formerly correct record that no longer applies should receive an end date rather than be deleted.
The Ground Truth dataset archives elevation points and attributes independently surveyed to verify EA time-stamped LIDAR.
Ground-truth collections were captured by independent surveyors.
A ground-truth survey contains a few hundred points.
Points are captured on flat, unambiguous surfaces.
Documented example surfaces include tarmac car parks and tennis courts.
Ground-truth points are captured using GPS.
Each ground-truth point has stated accuracy of plus or minus 3cm RMSE.
Ground-truth attributes include the geoidal model used.
A ground-truth survey may support multiple LIDAR surveys while less than five years old.
For coastal projects the reuse limit is three years.
Time-stamped LIDAR is compared with ground truth to assess RMSE.
A LIDAR survey must report error below plus or minus 15cm RMSE to pass the documented quality control.
The metadata states a 10cm threshold for standard deviation and random error.
The Ground Truth dataset reports no public-access constraint, subject to its licence.
The Ground Truth dataset is licensed under the Open Government Licence.
The metadata reports an annual update frequency.
The archive contains X, Y and Z survey points.
The dataset coordinate reference system is EPSG:27700.
A WMS service is published for the Ground Truth dataset.
A WFS service is published for the Ground Truth dataset.
An OGC API Features service is published for the Ground Truth dataset.
Full downloads are offered in geodatabase, GeoJSON, GeoPackage and shapefile packages.
The OS Terrain source DTM is captured as a triangulated irregular network.
The TIN is edited with mass points and breaklines and may also use automated photogrammetric techniques.
TIN triangles retain feature edges more accurately than a regular grid.
Source capture follows demanding height-capture specification rules.
Particular attention is paid to communication routes and height-significant features.
Both grid and contour products are interpolated from the source TIN.
The TIN is not distributed as the main product because it is not widely supported by GIS software.
OS Terrain 50 uses a more generalized representation suitable for small-scale products.
Minimum coverage extends to the low-water mark.
For England and Wales the coastal limit uses Mean Low Water.
For Scotland the coastal limit uses Mean Low Water Springs.
For mapped land within inland water, the minimum capture requirement is the outer edge.
The surrounding inland-water surface remains flat.
Other land captured automatically within inland water bodies is removed.
Source-height accuracy is classified for urban areas and major communication routes.
Source-height accuracy is separately classified for rural areas.
Source-height accuracy is separately classified for mountain and moorland.
Source X and Y coordinates are Eastings and Northings in OSGB36.
The source Z coordinate is a height in metres relative to the applicable datum.
Most source heights use Ordnance Survey Newlyn Datum.
A small number of offshore islands use a local height datum.
The bare-earth surface excludes buildings, supported structures and vegetation.
Ground-level obstructions such as sufficiently wide dams, breakwaters, groynes, revetments and earthworks are treated as bare-earth terrain.
Only terrain features expected to persist until the next revision period or longer are modelled.
Underground features are excluded from the DTM.
Overhead features are removed from the DTM.
The DTM is required to be free of spikes and wells that do not represent real terrain.
Supported structures are removed where they depart from bare earth and an air gap exists.
